newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova's post-independence leader ousted in poll.
newsitem.headline: Moldova's post-independence leader ousted in poll.

text.p: Petru Lucinschi, a leading communist turned social democrat, was elected president of Moldova after beating the former Soviet republic's first post- independence leader in a run-off vote on Sunday.

Preliminary results on Monday gave the 56-year-old chairman of parliament an eight-point winning margin over President Mircea Snegur, by 54 percent to 46. Turnout was 72 percent compared to 67 percent in the first round on November 17.

Lucinschi, a top Kremlin apparatchik in the final days of the Soviet Union, presents himself as a social democrat in the mould of reformed east European communists who have returned to power through the ballot box, as in Poland.
Favouring good relations with Moscow, he attacked as "savage capitalism" Snegur's plans for faster market reforms, such as the complete privatisation of Moldovan land.

Backed by much of the news media, Lucinschi played on fears in the Russian-speaking third of the population about Snegur's call for closer ties with Romania, from whose territory and people Stalin carved most of the republic in 1940.
Lucinschi says he will activate an existing accord to re- integrate the 700,000-strong Russian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 over fears of Romanian domination.
Hundreds of people were killed in fighting between Moldovan and Dnestr forces in 1992. Ultimately, Lucinschi wants the thousands of Russian peacekeeping troops in Dnestr to leave.
Dnestr did not vote on Sunday. The speaker of the breakaway territory's own parliament welcomed Lucinschi's election as a promising sign for talks on improving relations.
A bespectacled intellectual who trained as a historian, he advocates gradual economic reform, making use of international assistance and with a heavy dose of welfare guarantees.
Moldova's 4.3 million people have suffered a dramatic slump in living standards since independence in 1991.

Scoffing at the bluff and bulky Snegur's plans for ending dependence on Moscow, Lucinschi reminded Moldovans only Russia would keep supplying them vital energy on credit. They owe Russia some $600 million -- about a third of annual income.
Lucinschi accused Snegur, who has long been at loggerheads with his own government, of plotting to rig the vote or hold on to power with the help of sections of the security forces.

But the capital Chisinau was calm and state radio, quoting a presidential spokesman, said Snegur, 56, was leaving for Lisbon, where he is due to attend the summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Lucinschi's four-year term will begin on January 15.
Electoral officials noted no major violations of voting rules. OSCE observers also had no reports of serious trouble.
Moldovans hurrying to work on a wet Monday morning in the city centre took the news of change with an air of fatalism.
"I voted for Snegur," said Svetlana, a 27-year-old philologist. "But really, I don't think it makes a difference."
Valentina, who lives on a 90 lei ($18) a month pension, had voted for Lucinschi. "Now I hope he raises my pension and makes sure I get it every month, that's the main thing," she said.
Valeriu, a 40-year-old teacher, said: "What we need is someone really fresh, with new ideas to solve our problems."
"Lucinschi isn't really new," he added. "But perhaps he'll bring some new people into the government, a new generation."
Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who backed Lucinschi after being knocked out in the first round, has said he will resign.
Sangheli had been at odds with Snegur, leaving the administration partially paralysed.
